title: Injection Every 6 Months (Lenacapavir)
tagline: A shot just twice a year for year-round HIV protection
keyTakeaways: Get an injection just twice a year  - the least frequent dosing of any PrEP option
Shown to be highly effective in clinical trials, with a 96% reduction in HIV risk
Given as a small injection under the skin in the belly area
A newer option that offers maximum convenience for people who want minimal visits
If you stop, the medicine stays in your body for an extended period  - plan ahead with your provider

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Lenacapavir (brand name Sunlenca) is the newest form of PrEP and offers the longest gap between doses  - just one injection every 6 months. That means only two clinic visits a year for your PrEP. This option was developed for people who want highly effective HIV prevention with as little effort as possible between appointments. It was approved for PrEP use based on impressive results from large clinical trials.
keyPoints: One injection every 6 months (twice a year)
The newest and longest-acting PrEP option available
Given as a subcutaneous injection (a small shot under the skin in the belly area)
Approved based on strong clinical trial results showing high effectiveness

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: Lenacapavir belongs to a new class of HIV medications called capsid inhibitors. The capsid is the protective shell around HIV's genetic material  - think of it as the virus's armor. Lenacapavir targets this shell at multiple stages of the virus's life cycle, disrupting HIV's ability to infect cells and make copies of itself. Because it works differently from other PrEP medications, it's effective even against some HIV strains that are resistant to older drugs.
keyPoints: Targets the HIV capsid (the virus's protective outer shell)
Works at multiple stages of the virus's life cycle
Injected under the skin, where it forms a small depot that releases medicine slowly
Maintains protective drug levels for 6 full months between injections

sections.title: Dosing Schedule
sections.content: Getting started with lenacapavir involves a short oral loading phase before your first injection. This helps build up drug levels in your body quickly. Here's how the process works:
keyPoints: Step 1: Take 2 oral tablets on Day 1
Step 2: Take 1 oral tablet on Day 2
Step 3: Get your first injection on Day 28 (about 4 weeks later)
Step 4: Get your next injection 6 months after your first injection
Step 5: Continue with injections every 6 months from there

callouts.title: Why the oral loading?
callouts.text: The oral loading tablets help get the medicine into your system quickly while you wait for your first injection. It's just a few pills on two days  - much simpler than a month-long oral lead-in period.

callouts.title: Marking your calendar
callouts.text: With only two injection visits per year, it's easy to lose track. Schedule both appointments at the start of the year and set calendar reminders well in advance.

sections.title: Effectiveness
sections.content: Lenacapavir for PrEP was studied in two large clinical trials called PURPOSE 1 and PURPOSE 2. These trials showed that the twice-yearly injection was highly effective at preventing HIV. In the trials, lenacapavir reduced the risk of HIV by 96% compared to a background rate of infection  - meaning it prevented nearly all infections among participants who received it.
keyPoints: Reduced HIV risk by 96% in large clinical trials
Highly effective across diverse populations studied
No HIV infections occurred among participants who had detectable drug levels
One of the most effective PrEP options available

callouts.title: What the studies showed
callouts.text: In the PURPOSE clinical trials, the twice-yearly lenacapavir injection performed exceptionally well. Participants who received the injection were far less likely to acquire HIV compared to those who did not receive it.

sections.title: Side Effects
sections.content: The most common side effects are reactions at the injection site. Because the injection goes under the skin (rather than deep into muscle), you may notice a small bump or nodule at the injection site. For most people, these are mild and go away on their own.
keyPoints: Injection site reactions are the most common side effect  - small bumps, hardness, or tenderness at the injection site
These nodules are usually painless or mildly tender and typically resolve within weeks
Some people experience mild nausea or discomfort with the initial oral loading tablets
Serious side effects are uncommon
Your provider will check in on any side effects at your visits

callouts.title: About the injection site bumps
callouts.text: It's normal to feel a small lump under the skin where the injection was given. This is the medicine depot that will slowly release the drug over the next 6 months. These bumps are usually small and not noticeable to others.

sections.title: Getting Started
sections.content: Because lenacapavir for PrEP is newer, it may not be available at every clinic yet. Here's what to expect when getting started:
keyPoints: You'll get an HIV test to confirm you're HIV-negative
Your provider will review your health history and current medications (this is especially important for lenacapavir  - see Drug Interactions section)
You'll start the oral loading phase with tablets on Day 1 and Day 2
Your first injection will be scheduled for about 4 weeks later (Day 28)
The injection is given in the belly area (abdomen)  - it's a small subcutaneous shot
Your provider may have you stay briefly after the injection for observation

callouts.title: Availability
callouts.text: As a newer medication, lenacapavir for PrEP may not be available at all clinics yet. Ask your provider if they offer it, or check the Resources section for help finding a provider near you.

sections.title: Appointment Windows
sections.content: Your injection appointments will be scheduled every 6 months. While there is some flexibility, it's important to stay as close to your scheduled dates as possible to maintain full protection.
keyPoints: Target: every 6 months (about 26 weeks) between injections
Your provider will give you guidance on the acceptable window around your scheduled date
If you think you'll miss your appointment, call your provider as soon as possible to reschedule
Don't wait until you've missed your window  - reach out early if scheduling is tricky

callouts.title: Planning ahead
callouts.text: Since appointments are only twice a year, plan around holidays, vacations, or busy periods. Scheduling your next visit before you leave the clinic can help ensure you stay on track.

sections.title: Stopping Lenacapavir
sections.content: Like other injectable PrEP options, lenacapavir stays in your body for an extended period after your last injection. Because it's designed to last 6 months per dose, it takes a long time for the medication to fully leave your system. During this time, drug levels gradually decrease and may not provide full protection.
keyPoints: Lenacapavir remains in your body for a prolonged period after your last injection
During this tail period, drug levels may not be high enough for full protection
You'll need to use another form of HIV prevention during this transition
Your provider will help you create a plan for continued protection  - this might include switching to oral PrEP or using condoms consistently
Never stop without first talking to your provider

callouts.title: Plan your transition carefully
callouts.text: If you decide to stop lenacapavir, don't just skip your next appointment. Talk to your provider ahead of time so they can help you plan how to stay protected during the period when drug levels are declining. This is essential for your safety.

sections.title: Drug Interactions
sections.content: Lenacapavir can interact with certain other medications, which may affect how well it works. It's very important to tell your provider about everything you take  - including prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, and herbal supplements.
keyPoints: Some seizure/epilepsy medications may lower lenacapavir levels and reduce its effectiveness
Certain antibiotics used for tuberculosis can also interact with lenacapavir
The herbal supplement St. John's wort can reduce lenacapavir levels  - avoid using it while on this PrEP
Some supplements and herbal remedies may interact in ways that aren't fully known yet
Always tell your provider and pharmacist about everything you take before starting lenacapavir

callouts.title: Tell your provider about all your medications
callouts.text: Before starting lenacapavir, make a complete list of everything you take  - prescriptions, over-the-counter medications, vitamins, and any herbal or natural supplements like St. John's wort. Some of these can interfere with how well lenacapavir works.

sections.title: Cost & Access
sections.content: As a newer medication, lenacapavir's insurance coverage is still expanding. However, there are programs available to help with costs, and coverage is expected to grow as more providers begin offering it.
keyPoints: Insurance coverage varies  - check with your plan to see if lenacapavir for PrEP is covered
Gilead Sciences (the manufacturer) offers a patient assistance program for eligible individuals
Copay assistance programs may be available for those with insurance
Coverage is expected to expand as this option becomes more widely available
Ask your provider's office to help you navigate insurance and assistance options

callouts.title: Help with costs
callouts.text: If cost is a concern, don't give up. Ask your provider about Gilead's patient assistance programs, and check whether your insurance plan covers lenacapavir. Many people find a way to get their PrEP covered with some help.

sections.title: Common Questions
sections.content: Here are answers to some of the questions people ask most often about the twice-yearly lenacapavir injection.
keyPoints: Q: Does the injection hurt?  - A: It's a small subcutaneous injection in the belly area, similar to other shots given under the skin. Most people describe it as a quick pinch.
Q: Where exactly is the injection given?  - A: In the abdomen (belly area), just under the skin. Your provider will choose the best spot and alternate locations.
Q: Is this the same as the 2-month injection?  - A: No, lenacapavir (Sunlenca) is a different medication from cabotegravir (Apretude). They work differently and have different dosing schedules.
Q: Can I get this if I'm pregnant or planning pregnancy?  - A: Talk to your provider. They will help you weigh the benefits and considerations based on the latest available information.

Q: What if I want to switch to a different PrEP option later?  - A: You can switch, but because of the long-acting nature of this medication, work with your provider to plan the timing of your transition.

Q: Is this option available everywhere?  - A: Not yet  - it's newer and still becoming available at more clinics. Ask your provider or check PrEP locator tools to find a provider near you who offers it.
